metadata.synopsis: The SJC sustained Psiaki’s complaint and held that the CPC Session erred by ordaining and installing officers elected at a February 5, 2023 congregational meeting where the congregation’s bylaw excluded communing members under 18 from voting. Reading BCO 6-4, 25-1, and 25-7 together, the SJC ruled that all communing members are entitled to vote and that local bylaws cannot impose an age restriction; the “good and regular standing” language addresses censure, not age. The decision did not annul the completed ordination/installation, but required future elections and installations to comply with the Constitution.

relationships.title: Troxell v. Presbytery of the Southwest
relationships.disposition: Complaint partially sustained; challenged action annulled

metadata.synopsis: A complaint challenged Presbytery’s institution of two charges against a teaching elder and related pretrial actions. The SJC annulled the household-management charge because process began fifteen months after the alleged offense and the record showed no recently flagrant, newly evident, or continuing offense under BCO 32-20. It also held that declaring the elder not in good standing removed rights without process, but left his properly imposed suspension effective. It rejected objections to discussion, questioning, and the timely submission charge, which could proceed without any determination of guilt.

provisions.title: Section 14-3
provisions.body: When an emergency shall require a meeting of the General Assembly earlier than the time to which it stands adjourned, the moderator shall issue a call for a special meeting at the request or with the concurrence of ten percent (10%) of the commissioners who had seats in the Assembly at its preceding meeting, of whom at least ten shall be teaching elders and at least ten ruling elders, representing at least one-third (1/3) of the Presbyteries. Should the moderator be for any reason unable to act, the stated clerk shall under the same requirements issue the call. The members of the special meeting shall be the commissioners elected to the preceding meeting of the Assembly or their alternates. A Session, however, shall have the right to elect a commissioner or alternate in the stead of one who had died since the last meeting of the Assembly, or of one who has notified the moderator of the Session of his inability to serve. Notice of the special meeting shall be sent not less than twenty (20) days in advance to each commissioner and to the moderator of each Presbytery. In the notice the purpose of the meeting is to be stated and no other business is to be transacted.

metadata.synopsis: The SJC sustained TE Craig Sheppard's complaint against Highlands Presbytery. It held that Presbytery erred when its Judicial Commission found a strong presumption of guilt but, instead of instituting process under BCO 31-2, directed pastoral reconciliation and conditioned later process on its success; that motion also impaired the accused's right against self-incrimination. It further held that BCO 32-20's one-year time bar had run and that the 2022 amendment did not apply retroactively, so Presbytery is debarred from prosecuting the allegations. Four commissioners dissented, disputing the BCO 32-20 ruling.

metadata.synopsis: The SJC sustained Psiaki’s complaint and held that the CPC Session erred by ordaining and installing officers elected at a February 5, 2023 congregational meeting where the congregation’s bylaw excluded communing members under 18 from voting. Reading BCO 6-4, 25-1, and 25-7 together, the SJC ruled that all communing members are entitled to vote and that local bylaws cannot impose an age restriction; the “good and regular standing” language addresses censure, not age. The decision did not annul the completed ordination/installation, but required future elections and installations to comply with the Constitution.

provisions.title: Section 14-6
provisions.body: The General Assembly shall have power: a. To receive and issue* all appeals, references, and complaints regularly brought before it from the lower courts; to bear testimony against error in doctrine and immorality in practice, injuriously affecting the Church; to decide in all controversies respecting doctrine and discipline; * [Editor's note: "Issue" means "settling the issue of the case".] b. To give its advice and instruction, in conformity with the Constitution, in all cases submitted to it; c. To review the records of the Presbyteries, to take care that the lower courts observe the Constitution; to redress whatever they may have done contrary to order; d. To devise measures for promoting the prosperity and enlargement of the Church; e. To erect new Presbyteries, and unite and divide those which were erected with their consent; f. To institute and superintend the agencies necessary in the general work of evangelization; to appoint ministers of such labors as fall under its jurisdiction; g. To suppress schismatical contentions and disputations, according to the rules provided therefor; h. To receive under its jurisdiction, with the consent of three-fourths (3/4) of the Presbyteries, other ecclesiastical bodies whose organization is conformed to the doctrine and order of this Church; to authorize Presbyteries to exercise similar power in receiving bodies suited to become constituents of those courts, and lying within their geographical bounds respectively; i. To superintend the affairs of the whole Church; j. To correspond with other churches; to unite with other ecclesiastical bodies whose organization is conformed to the doctrines and order of this Church, such union to be effected by a mode of procedure defined in BCO 26; and k. In general to recommend measures for the promotion of charity, truth and holiness through all the churches under its care.

relationships.title: BCO 40-5 Matter re Metropolitan NY

metadata.synopsis: A BCO 40-5 citation arose from Metro New York Presbytery's failure to redress a session that allowed a woman to expound Scripture in place of the sermon preceding the Lord's Supper, held services without preaching, and celebrated the Supper without a preceding sermon. The SJC remitted the matter to the presbytery for constitutional resolution because the session's later no-exception response was clearly inadequate and the unapproved minutes were unclear. Presbytery must complete its work with TE Higgins and Trinity Presbyterian Church's session and report to the 51st General Assembly. A separate procedural note questioned the Assembly's direct referral but did not void it.

relationships.title: BCO 40-5 Matter re NW Georgia
relationships.disposition: BCO 40-5 ruling found egregious constitutional error and fully redressed the reported matter, but denied the requested annulment of the installations.

metadata.synopsis: Presbytery approved calls and installed three associate pastors after a constitutionally deficient election. The SJC found egregious error, including slate voting, a standing rather than ballot vote, and failure to determine and record the number of voters present under the then-current rule. It nevertheless denied the requested annulment of the installations because PCA judicial proceedings supplied no precedent and the remedy's legitimacy was doubtful. The SJC stayed further proceedings and declared the report concluded.

metadata.synopsis: Biese and others complained that Tennessee Valley Presbytery erred by approving Redeemer Church session minutes without exception—minutes noting a youth Super Bowl party—and by denying their complaint seeking a Sabbath exception. The SJC denied the complaint: because Presbytery gave no reasons for its actions, the record was insufficient to find it erred in interpreting the Constitution. A concurrence said the denial did not decide the Sabbath merits; a dissent would have held the complaint judicially out of order for lack of SJC jurisdiction over presbytery record review.

The SJC held the filing out of order: under RAO 16-10.c and OMSJC Chapter 15, BCO Chapter 40 matters come to it only by General Assembly referral. It did not decide the merits, but noted that without proper notice Lewis remains a member unless she joined another church. Dissents disputed that limitation and cited past direct reviews.

topics: fundamentals of the system of doctrine
metadata.synopsis: An SJC complaint alleged that Ohio Valley Presbytery failed to comply with the SJC's prior remand in Case 2014-01, which required it to 'hear further' from TE Charles Hickey about his changed view on Larger Catechism 177. The SJC denied the complaint. It held that the prior decision neither sustained nor denied the original complaint and prescribed no particular examination procedure; Hickey's nine pages of additional affirmations, exegesis, and answers constituted hearing further, and he addressed the five identified areas at least in part. A concurrence believed the SJC could also have adjudicated the confessional-difference merits; a dissent would have found noncompliance and reached the merits.

relationships.title: Barnes v. Heartland Presbytery

topics: fundamentals of the system of doctrine
metadata.synopsis: Heartland Presbytery granted a transferring OPC teaching elder an exception to WCF 19, judging his stated differences 'more than semantic but not out of accord with any fundamental.' The SJC sustained a complaint not against the merits of that judgment but against the sufficiency of the record supporting it. It held Presbytery clearly erred by failing to develop a sufficient record: the presbyters as a whole did not receive OPCUS's adverse actions, its teaching restriction, or the elder's longer paper. Remanded for those materials and release documentation to be included in the minutes. A concurrence addressed deference; four dissenters found no clear error.

relationships.title: Brown v. Northern California Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: Brown challenged Presbytery’s abstract approval of six views concerning diaconal practice. The SJC sustained the consolidated complaints and annulled Presbytery’s action because a church court cannot issue a binding decree apart from properly exercising jurisdiction over specific persons. Constitutional conformity must instead be determined through authorized examination or judicial processes. The judgment deliberately left unresolved whether any of the six views themselves were faithful to the Constitution; the detailed view-by-view analysis appeared only in a concurring opinion.

relationships.title: Jones v. Louisiana

occurrences.excerpt: That, as Louisiana Presbytery has not completed an adequate examination of TE Wilkins’ views, the SJC hereby finds that the matters be redressed (BCO 40-5, para. 2, clause 1; cf., SJCM 16.9(a); BCO 14-6, a-b) by the following:

metadata.synopsis: Louisiana Presbytery’s refusal to institute process after examining Steve Wilkins’s Federal Vision teachings was challenged for applying the wrong constitutional standard and overlooking a strong presumption that some views were out of conformity with the Westminster Standards. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled Presbytery’s denial. A “difference” need not expressly contradict the Standards; Presbytery must independently investigate and classify it rather than accept the member’s assurance or shift the burden to objectors. The ruling did not adjudicate Wilkins’s guilt; the Central Carolina memorial remained before the SJC.

relationships.title: Memorial of Central Carolina v. Louisiana

occurrences.excerpt: That, as Louisiana Presbytery has not completed an adequate examination of TE Wilkins’ views, the Standing Judicial Commission hereby finds that the matters be redressed (BCO 40-5, para. 2, clause 1; cf., SJCM 16.9(a); BCO 14-6, a-b) by the following:

metadata.synopsis: In a BCO 40-5 memorial, Central Carolina Presbytery alleged that Louisiana Presbytery had exonerated TE J. Steven Wilkins despite his published views on election, the church, perseverance, assurance, and baptism allegedly contradicting the Westminster Standards. The SJC sustained the memorial’s gravity and found Presbytery failed to show due diligence, ordering a recorded examination, formal responses, and report. Presbytery later met the procedural directives, but the SJC relied on Case 2007-8’s substantive finding, cited Presbytery under BCO 40-5, and appointed a prosecutor for Case 2007-14.

provisions.title: Section 14-7
provisions.body: Actions of the General Assembly pursuant to the provision of BCO 14-6 such as deliverances, resolutions, overtures, and judicial decisions are to be given due and serious consideration by the Church and its lower courts when deliberating matters related to such action. Judicial decisions shall be binding and conclusive on the parties who are directly involved in the matter being adjudicated, and may be appealed to in subsequent similar cases as to any principle which may have been decided. (See BCO 3-5 and 6, and WCF 31:3.)

Klett et al. complained. The SJC sustained the complaint: Smith's written views affirmed continuing non-general revelation and treated prophecy and tongues as public-worship elements, contrary to WCF 1 and 21, so Presbytery erred under BCO 21-4.f. relationships.title: Sheppard v. Highlands Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: The SJC sustained TE Craig Sheppard's complaint against Highlands Presbytery. It held that Presbytery erred when its Judicial Commission found a strong presumption of guilt but, instead of instituting process under BCO 31-2, directed pastoral reconciliation and conditioned later process on its success; that motion also impaired the accused's right against self-incrimination. It further held that BCO 32-20's one-year time bar had run and that the 2022 amendment did not apply retroactively, so Presbytery is debarred from prosecuting the allegations. Four commissioners dissented, disputing the BCO 32-20 ruling.

provisions.title: Chapter 15 · Ecclesiastical Commissions
provisions.body:
BCO 15-1

A commission differs from an ordinary committee in that while a committee is appointed to examine, consider, and report, a commission is authorized to deliberate upon and conclude the business referred to it. A commission shall keep a full record of its proceedings, which shall be submitted to the court appointing it. Upon such submission this record shall be entered on the minutes of the court appointing, the date of the submission being the date of "the meeting of the court" for filing requirements under the rules of discipline, with exception of the "notification" dates of BCO 42-4 and 43-3. The effective date of dismissal of a commission of Session or Presbytery shall be not before the time allowed for the filing of a complaint or appeal against that commission's decision has expired. Any complaint or appeal so timely filed, shall be adjudicated by that commission until the matter is settled by that commission or a higher court. When a commission is appointed to serve as an interim Session, its actions are the actions of a Session, not a Presbytery. Every commission of a Presbytery or Session must submit complete minutes and a report of its activities at least once annually to the court which commissioned it.

BCO 15-2

Among the matters that may be properly executed by commissions are the taking of the testimony in judicial cases, the ordination of ministers, the installation of ministers, the visitation of portions of the church affected with disorder, and the organization of new churches. Every commission appointed by Presbytery shall consist of at least two teaching elders and two ruling elders, and the quorum shall be one more than half its membership unless otherwise determined by the Presbytery. However, should a Presbytery clothe a commission with judicial powers and authority to conduct judicial process, or with power to ordain or install a teaching elder of the Gospel, the quorum of such commission shall not be less than two teaching elders and two ruling elders. The quorum for a commission appointed as an interim session need not conform to the requirements of a judicial commission, but only to those of a session (BCO 12-1). When the ordination of a minister is committed to a commission, the Presbytery itself shall conduct the previous examination.

BCO 15-3

Presbytery as a whole may hear a case, with or without process (BCO 31-38), a reference (BCO 41), an appeal (BCO 42), a complaint (BCO 43), a BCO 40-5 proceeding, or a request to assume original jurisdiction (BCO 33-1) properly before it, or it may of its own motion commit such a case to a commission. Such a commission shall be appointed by the Presbytery from its members other than members of the Session of the church from which the case comes up. The commission shall try the case in the manner presented by the Rules of Discipline and shall submit to the Presbytery a full statement of the case and the judgment rendered. The judgment of the commission shall be the decision of the Presbytery, and the statement of the case and judgment printed in its minutes.

BCO 15-4

The General Assembly shall elect a Standing Judicial Commission to which it shall commit all matters governed by the Rules of Discipline, except for the annual review of Presbytery records, which may come before the Assembly. This commission shall consist of twenty-four (24) members divided into four classes of three teaching elders and three ruling elders in each class. Each class shall serve a four-year term and each subsequent Assembly shall declare the Standing Judicial Commission as a whole to be its commission. Nominations and vacancies shall be filled according to BCO 14-1(11), with nominations allowed from the floor. No person may be elected if there is already a member of the commission from the same Presbytery; but if a person is elected and changes Presbytery, he may continue to serve his full term. No person may serve concurrently on the General Assembly's Standing Judicial Commission and any of the General Assembly's permanent committees.

BCO 15-5

a. In the cases committed to it, the Standing Judicial Commission shall have the judicial powers and be governed by the judicial procedures of the General Assembly. The decision of the Standing Judicial Commission shall be the final decision of the General Assembly except as set forth below, to which there may be no complaint or appeal. Members of the Standing Judicial Commission may file concurring or dissenting opinions, or a minority report as set forth in (c) below. The General Assembly may direct the Standing Judicial Commission to retry a case if upon the review of its minutes exceptions are taken with respect to that case. b. In each case the Standing Judicial Commission shall issue a summary of the facts, a statement of the issues, its judgment and its reasoning, together with any concurring or dissenting opinions, all of which shall be entered on the minutes of the General Assembly and shall be reported by the Stated Clerk to the next General Assembly. The judgment shall be effective from the time of its announcement to the parties. c.(1) If, within twenty-four (24) hours of the time of adjournment of a Standing Judicial Commission meeting at which a final decision was rendered in a case, at least one-third (1/3) of the voting members of the Standing Judicial Commission file written notice of their intention to file a minority decision with the Stated Clerk of the General Assembly, and within twenty (20) days from the adjournment do file such a minority decision, such minority decision shall be considered a minority report and shall be referred, with the report of the Standing Judicial Commission, to the General Assembly. In each instance "file" shall be understood as defined by the Operating Manual for Standing Judicial Commission. (2) No such reference* from the Standing Judicial Commission shall be considered by the General Assembly unless the report of the Standing Judicial Commission and the minority report have been mailed to the clerk of Session of each church at least thirty (30) days prior to the meeting of the General Assembly. (3) The Assembly shall act upon such a reference* from the Standing Judicial Commission, in each case without question, discussion, debate, or amendment, as follows: *NOTE: It was the opinion of the 26th General Assembly that "reference" is NOT to be understood as the technical term "reference" in BCO 41-1. (a) The Standing Judicial Commission shall have 30 minutes to present its decision to the Assembly. (b) The minority shall have 30 minutes to present its decision to the Assembly. (c) The Standing Judicial Commission shall have 10 minutes to reply to the minority report. (d) The decision of the minority shall be proposed and the General Assembly shall, without question, discussion, debate, or amendment approve or disapprove of the minority report. (e) If the General Assembly disapproves the minority report, the General Assembly shall take up the decision of the Standing Judicial Commission and without question, discussion, debate, or amendment, approve or disapprove of the decision of the Standing Judicial Commission. (4) If the General Assembly approves of a proposed decision, it shall be the decision of the General Assembly, and printed in its minutes. There may be no complaint or appeal from such a final decision of the General Assembly. If the General Assembly finally disapproves of both proposed decisions, it must set the case for hearing before the General Assembly or a special commission appointed by it, and in either instance the case shall be tried on the record as delivered to the Stated Clerk. Any such special commission shall then proceed to consider the case and shall report its decision, in like manner, to the General Assembly for its approval or disapproval. In any event, the full record of the case, including written testimony of witnesses, all documents, exhibits and papers shall be delivered to the Stated Clerk for permanent preservation.

BCO 15-6

The General Assembly shall have power to commit to a commission, consisting of not less than three elders, the task of forming a provisional Presbytery in a foreign country where there exists no compatible indigenous presbyterian and reformed Church. Such a commission shall have authority to act as the Presbytery in all matters pertaining to the establishment and ordering of a national Church and shall report annually to the General Assembly. The commission shall be dissolved when there are at least three national teaching elders and three organized churches under its care, and these shall then constitute a separate national Church.

provisions.title: Section 15-1
provisions.body: A commission differs from an ordinary committee in that while a committee is appointed to examine, consider, and report, a commission is authorized to deliberate upon and conclude the business referred to it. A commission shall keep a full record of its proceedings, which shall be submitted to the court appointing it. Upon such submission this record shall be entered on the minutes of the court appointing, the date of the submission being the date of "the meeting of the court" for filing requirements under the rules of discipline, with exception of the "notification" dates of BCO 42-4 and 43-3. The effective date of dismissal of a commission of Session or Presbytery shall be not before the time allowed for the filing of a complaint or appeal against that commission's decision has expired. Any complaint or appeal so timely filed, shall be adjudicated by that commission until the matter is settled by that commission or a higher court. When a commission is appointed to serve as an interim Session, its actions are the actions of a Session, not a Presbytery. Every commission of a Presbytery or Session must submit complete minutes and a report of its activities at least once annually to the court which commissioned it.

The SJC denied the complaint, specifically holding that Woodward lacked standing because he was not under Presbytery’s jurisdiction. It also held that BCO 31-2 prescribes no interview requirement or fixed timeline and found no clear constitutional error warranting departure from ordinary deference to Presbytery.

metadata.synopsis: Smith challenged Presbytery’s reversal of a finding that an elder’s race-and-IQ views did not create a strong presumption of guilt and its immediate judgment against those views. The SJC upheld the reversal as a discretionary determination, without addressing its merits, but annulled the declaration against the views because a strong-presumption finding required judicial process. On remand, Presbytery was to commence process against the elder or rescind that finding and drop the matter. The ruling did not restrict Presbytery’s ability to adopt general position statements outside an investigation.

metadata.synopsis: Chastain appealed Heritage Presbytery’s 2006 excommunication and deposition. The SJC held the appeal judicially out of order because Chastain had renounced PCA jurisdiction on May 8, 2006. Consequently, Presbytery’s later proceedings were moot and SJC 2005-1 remained in effect. The SJC did not reach the merits. A concurrence questioned the discipline process after renunciation; a dissent argued the majority lacked constitutional authority to recognize unilateral withdrawal and thereby undercut discipline.

metadata.synopsis: A minister challenged Presbytery’s denial of his complaints concerning a congregational petition and an Administrative Commission’s actions. The SJC sustained both issues: the petition should first have gone to the Session, and Presbytery and its Commission committed additional constitutional errors. Those errors did not excuse his refusal to obey Presbytery, however. Because he had been deposed in Case 2005-8, further action was moot; the SJC granted no remedy, vacatur, or remand.

metadata.synopsis: The Chins complained to the SJC after Covenant Presbytery denied their complaint against Covenant Presbyterian Church Session's refusal to examine their young children for admission to the Lord's Supper. The SJC did not sustain the complaint. Its adopted reasoning held that BCO 57-2 leaves the time for examining young persons to the Session's prudence and imposes no mandate to examine every child put forward; if the Session decides the time has come, careful examination is required. The dissent read BCO 57-1 as requiring examination of covenant children seeking admission.

metadata.synopsis: A church session suspended a member from the Lord's Table and found her guilty of contumacy. The chairman of Presbytery's Judicial Business Committee advised her that her appeal was out of order; Presbytery later ruled her complaint untimely. The SJC sustained her complaint: she had submitted to regular trial, making her appeal in order under BCO 42-2, and her complaint was timely after Presbytery's advice caused the appeal to be renamed. It remanded for Presbytery to adjudicate the appeal. Filing the appeal suspended the Lord's Table censure pending final adjudication; the SJC questioned the contumacy ruling.

metadata.synopsis: The SJC sustained a session's timely complaint that Louisiana Presbytery barred one of its members from the Lord's Table after assuming original jurisdiction. Under BCO 33-1, a presbytery may assume jurisdiction only when the session 'refuses to act'; because the session had investigated and found no strong presumption of guilt, it acted, so LAP never acquired jurisdiction. The censure was therefore a nullity, and the member remained under his session. The SJC also held the jurisdictional assumption reviewable despite no timely complaint against it. Three commissioners dissented.

relationships.title: Nickoley and Stephens v. Southwest Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: Complainants challenged Southwest Presbytery's January 1991 actions: withdrawing charges against two ruling elders, dissolving Pastor Pollock's pastoral relationship, and rescinding its suspension of Covenant PC's session. The SJC did not sustain the complaint and affirmed. It held the BCO gives no presbytery authority to suspend a session or act as a Session pro tem without formal congregational consent; BCO 31-1 left the elder charges with the session, so they were never validly before Presbytery; the dissolution challenge was moot after Pollock left the PCA, though Presbytery acted correctly on the congregation's request.

relationships.title: Chappell v. Eastern Carolina Presbytery

topics: suspension of session without due process
metadata.synopsis: Ruling Elder Chappell complained against Eastern Carolina Presbytery's Commission, which had suspended the session of Fuller Memorial Presbyterian Church and constituted itself as a 'Session Pro Tem' without due process or congregational consent. The SJC sustained the complaint, holding that the BCO grants no authority for a presbytery to depose a session and act in its place, that suspension requires due process, and that the congregation has an inalienable right to be governed by officers it has chosen.

provisions.title: Section 15-2
provisions.body: Among the matters that may be properly executed by commissions are the taking of the testimony in judicial cases, the ordination of ministers, the installation of ministers, the visitation of portions of the church affected with disorder, and the organization of new churches. Every commission appointed by Presbytery shall consist of at least two teaching elders and two ruling elders, and the quorum shall be one more than half its membership unless otherwise determined by the Presbytery. However, should a Presbytery clothe a commission with judicial powers and authority to conduct judicial process, or with power to ordain or install a teaching elder of the Gospel, the quorum of such commission shall not be less than two teaching elders and two ruling elders. The quorum for a commission appointed as an interim session need not conform to the requirements of a judicial commission, but only to those of a session (BCO 12-1). When the ordination of a minister is committed to a commission, the Presbytery itself shall conduct the previous examination.

metadata.synopsis: A ruling elder challenged Session’s elder-term proposal and its creation of Judicial and Governance Commissions. The SJC denied the first two claims: the Constitution does not regulate elder terms, and the Judicial Commission’s assigned business was sufficiently defined. It sustained the Governance Commission claim because sweeping authority and reversed delegation allowed that body to function as Session itself, contrary to BCO 15-1. Session’s third motion was annulled, but Session remained free to adopt a narrower, constitutionally compliant plan.

relationships.title: Speck v. Missouri Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: Speck challenged Missouri Presbytery’s approval of six theological judgments concerning teachings at Revoice 18, its rejection of his procedural point of order, and its refusal to debate gay-couple adoption. The SJC sustained only the first issue, particularly as to Judgments 2, 3, and 5: Presbytery improperly imported BCO 34-5’s ministerial-process standard into court review and then inadequately addressed identified errors affecting church peace and purity. It rejected the procedural and adoption claims and remanded for a focused new hearing under BCO 11-3, 11-4, and 13-9(f).

metadata.synopsis: Malone challenged Presbytery’s approval of a commission’s judgment and indefinite suspension imposed without process. The SJC sustained the complaint in part and vacated the judgment and censure: the commission had authority only to investigate, and Malone’s general acknowledgments neither confessed specific charges nor showed intent to waive process under BCO 38-1. Presbytery could begin anew under proper procedures. The SJC rejected Malone’s claim that suggested steps evidencing repentance improperly bound him, treating them as noncompulsory pastoral advice.

relationships.title: Harwell et al. v. Nashville Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: Complainants sought review of Nashville Presbytery's August 9, 2016 actions but filed directly with the SJC instead of first with Presbytery. The SJC held the complaint judicially out of order and unable to be put in order: the initial filing was not a complaint against an act or decision (BCO 43-1) but suggested charges or an investigation request (BCO 31-2); BCO 43-2 required prior filing with Presbytery, and the sixty-day period had run. The complaint was dismissed without a merits ruling.

metadata.synopsis: Did a presbytery violate the BCO or clearly err by dissolving a congregation without its consent? The SJC said no and denied the complaint. On the constitutional issue, it held that BCO 13-9.f grants dissolution power and BCO 40-6 does not impose formal process for it. On the discretionary issue, it found no clear error in the record. The denial left dissolution in place and warned that such action still requires sufficient justification and prudent, reviewable procedure.

metadata.synopsis: The complaint challenged Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery’s November 17, 2012 vote adopting its Complaint Commission’s recommendation to institute process and try TE David Swavely. The SJC did not sustain it. Although the record showed possible procedural irregularities—including unauthorized circulation of an earlier complaint—the SJC found no reversible error: presbyteries receive deference on factual records and broad latitude to judge the sufficiency of investigations. The recommendation to proceed to trial stands, subject to later parliamentary action. The SJC did not decide Swavely’s guilt.

relationships.title: Dunn v. Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: The SJC held TE Dwight Dunn's complaint administratively out of order under OMSJC 9.1 and directed Presbytery to remedy the deficiencies by its next Stated Meeting before further action under OMSJC 9.2. The original complaint had been transmitted to the Faith Church Commission by the Stated Clerk, not committed by Presbytery motion as BCO 15-3 requires, and after the Commission denied it, the Commission did not seek Presbytery approval of its judgment. Because Presbytery had not acted, the SJC complaint was premature; no merits were reached.

metadata.synopsis: After Korean Eastern Presbytery tried, convicted, deposed, and excommunicated TE Eliot Lee, the SJC sustained his appeal and reversed the disposition and excommunication. The decisive reason was procedural: the record did not show timely service of the indictment/citations or the required 14-day trial notice, violating BCO 32-3, 32-7, and 32-10. Under BCO 42-9, the SJC rendered the decision it thought should have been made, finding no strong presumption of guilt under BCO 31-2 justified formal process; it added pastoral counsel, expressly not censure.

relationships.title: Linton v. Western Carolina Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: Robert Woodward challenged Presbytery’s acceptance of a finding that accusations against TE Craig Bulkeley did not raise a strong presumption of guilt, alleging investigators never heard his evidence. The SJC denied the complaint, specifically holding that Woodward lacked standing because he was not under Presbytery’s jurisdiction. It also held that BCO 31-2 prescribes no interview requirement or fixed timeline and found no clear constitutional error warranting departure from ordinary deference to Presbytery.

metadata.synopsis: Lee challenged Korean Eastern Presbytery’s ratification and filing of a New Jersey lawsuit through a commission acting for the local church, seeking civil adjudication of who was the rightful pastor and who could act as the church’s session. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled Presbytery’s decision in whole. PCA courts have moral and spiritual, not civil coercive, authority and cannot sue to enforce ecclesiastical decisions. The ruling does not prohibit litigation over purely civil matters and did not condemn the commission’s original appointment.

metadata.synopsis: After a church member and deacon was excommunicated by his session, he appealed to Evangel Presbytery. Presbytery found the appeal in order and appointed a commission, but then rescinded that action and never adjudicated the appeal. The SJC held Presbytery erred by failing to notify the appellant of the appeal hearing and by failing to adjudicate an appeal properly before it. It remanded under BCO 42-9 for proper adjudication and made no ruling on the remaining session-related merits issues.

relationships.title: Nickoley v. Rocky Mountain

metadata.synopsis: Rocky Mountain Presbytery cited Pastor Bruce Nickoley for contumacy during his trial, after he allegedly refused to tell his congregation to stop picketing, and immediately deposed him without a hearing. On appeal, the SJC sustained the appeal, holding the Presbytery misapplied BCO provisions on confession, citation, refusal to testify, and deposition; Nickoley neither confessed nor refused to appear. Although presbyteries have general authority to maintain order, serious charges require due process. The SJC remanded, recommending either a new process beginning with BCO §32-3 or revocation of the deposition and reinstatement.

provisions.title: Section 15-3
provisions.body: Presbytery as a whole may hear a case, with or without process (BCO 31-38), a reference (BCO 41), an appeal (BCO 42), a complaint (BCO 43), a BCO 40-5 proceeding, or a request to assume original jurisdiction (BCO 33-1) properly before it, or it may of its own motion commit such a case to a commission. Such a commission shall be appointed by the Presbytery from its members other than members of the Session of the church from which the case comes up. The commission shall try the case in the manner presented by the Rules of Discipline and shall submit to the Presbytery a full statement of the case and the judgment rendered. The judgment of the commission shall be the decision of the Presbytery, and the statement of the case and judgment printed in its minutes.

relationships.title: Sears v. Nashville Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: TE Ian Sears appealed his deposition by Nashville Presbytery, which handled the case as a BCO 38-1 case without process after he signed a written confession of guilt for two incidents of sexual misconduct in 2010 and 2011. The SJC unanimously denied the appeal on all five specifications of error, affirming the Presbytery's judgment and the validity of the BCO 38-1 process, including its procedures for drafting the confession and refusing to allow Sears to withdraw it after censure was imposed.

relationships.title: Suh v. Korean Southeastern Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: TE Sam Jung Suh appealed his indefinite suspension by Korean Southeastern Presbytery following a trial on charges of financial misconduct. The SJC reversed the conviction in whole, finding that the pre-investigative and BCO 31-2 investigation phases were marred by grave constitutional errors including failure to comply with BCO 27-5, failure to demand satisfactory explanations from TE Suh, improper expansion of the investigation, and absence of a valid antecedent condition necessary to institute process; multiple dissents argued the SJC should have deferred to the lower court's factual findings and trial verdict.

metadata.synopsis: A ruling elder challenged Session’s elder-term proposal and its creation of Judicial and Governance Commissions. The SJC denied the first two claims: the Constitution does not regulate elder terms, and the Judicial Commission’s assigned business was sufficiently defined. It sustained the Governance Commission claim because sweeping authority and reversed delegation allowed that body to function as Session itself, contrary to BCO 15-1. Session’s third motion was annulled, but Session remained free to adopt a narrower, constitutionally compliant plan.

relationships.title: Dudt v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery

topics: express vs. implied will of session
metadata.synopsis: A ruling elder appealed convictions for distributing an SJC decision contrary to Session's will and for allegedly false, divisive statements in an email opposing a pastoral-election proposal. The SJC sustained the appeal, reversed Session and Presbytery in whole, rendered not guilty, removed the indefinite suspension, and restored him to office. Session could not bind conscience without scriptural authority, and no express prohibition or proof of falsity existed. Many other specifications were rejected; a concurrence cautioned that such emails are rarely wise.

relationships.title: Speck v. Missouri Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: Speck challenged Missouri Presbytery’s approval of six theological judgments concerning teachings at Revoice 18, its rejection of his procedural point of order, and its refusal to debate gay-couple adoption. The SJC sustained only the first issue, particularly as to Judgments 2, 3, and 5: Presbytery improperly imported BCO 34-5’s ministerial-process standard into court review and then inadequately addressed identified errors affecting church peace and purity. It rejected the procedural and adoption claims and remanded for a focused new hearing under BCO 11-3, 11-4, and 13-9(f).

metadata.synopsis: Ryan Speck challenged Missouri Presbytery’s BCO 31-2 investigation and its refusal to commence process against Greg Johnson on four allegations concerning same-sex attraction as sin, identity in Christ, sanctification, and fitness for office. The SJC denied the complaint in full. It found no clear procedural error and held that Johnson’s explanations and clarifications made Presbytery’s non-indictment judgments reasonable. No trial was ordered. The ruling neither adjudged Johnson guilty nor endorsed every statement or broader constitutional position concerning same-sex attraction.

metadata.synopsis: Malone challenged Presbytery’s approval of a commission’s judgment and indefinite suspension imposed without process. The SJC sustained the complaint in part and vacated the judgment and censure: the commission had authority only to investigate, and Malone’s general acknowledgments neither confessed specific charges nor showed intent to waive process under BCO 38-1. Presbytery could begin anew under proper procedures. The SJC rejected Malone’s claim that suggested steps evidencing repentance improperly bound him, treating them as noncompulsory pastoral advice.

metadata.synopsis: Marusich challenged Presbytery’s receipt of a commission’s finding that accusations against a teaching elder did not establish a strong presumption of guilt, and the commission’s failure to provide minutes or a full report. Without answering either issue or identifying an error, the SJC remanded for a new BCO 31-2 investigation, a narrative of the evidence, and a recommendation for Presbytery’s consideration under regular orders. The decision expressly establishes no general rule for BCO 31-2 investigations.

The SJC sustained the complaint, annulled Presbytery’s approval, and returned the matter to the PJC. Because he admitted only some indicted charges, his negotiated confession could not satisfy BCO 38-1 and the conversion prejudiced his rights. The PJC may dismiss or proceed under BCO 32; the ruling does not decide whether conversion is ever permissible.

The SJC sustained RE Scott Dailey's complaint against that action. BCO 43-3 allows higher-court review only if the lower court denies a complaint or fails to consider it by its next stated meeting. The adopted judgment held that the 147-page record showed Presbytery fulfilled its BCO 31-2 investigatory duty and did not show it erred in judgment when it declined process; the complaint was denied 20-0-1. Concurring opinions raised concerns about committee recusal, record clarity, and exegetical uses of Scripture, but they were separate and did not alter the denial.

The complaint alleged the investigating committee lacked authority for judicial process, no written report existed, and the procedure and wording violated BCO 31-2. The Commission held a committee recommendation is not judicial action, no special instruction was required, the BCO 31-2 steps were followed, and the wording did not violate the accused’s rights.

metadata.synopsis: Did a presbytery fail in its duty to condemn erroneous opinions by acquitting a minister on theological-error charges? The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the acquittal undisturbed. A complaint against a not-guilty verdict cannot provoke a retrial at the superior court; under BCO 43 the superior court may only annul or remand, not reverse, and the complainant bore the burden to show error from the record. The record contained the defendant's testimony, including recantations or clarifications, Defense Exhibit 1, and witness testimony sufficient to refrain from contradicting the trial court. The SJC expressly did not decide the defendant's actual views. A separate concurrence elaborated deference standards but did not change the judgment.

metadata.synopsis: A complainant challenged Nashville Presbytery's handling of allegations against a teaching elder. The SJC held the matter judicially out of order and dismissed it, finding the original filing with the church session was not a BCO 43-1 complaint because the session lacked jurisdiction over the teaching elder. Presbytery properly treated the allegations as BCO 31-2/34-1 reports, and the complainant, not a Nashville member, lacked standing to complain about that new action. A nine-member dissent argued the filing of charges conferred standing under prior SJC cases.

relationships.title: Fordice v. Pacific Northwest Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: A church member challenged Presbytery’s denial of his complaint after it resolved accusations against a minister through a BCO 38-1 confession rather than trial. The SJC held that using confession without process was not itself error, but the statement and confession failed to correlate with and address the specific allegations. It sustained the complaint, annulled the denial, and remanded for Presbytery to amend the documents, institute process, reactivate the investigative committee, or otherwise respond directly and specifically to the unresolved allegations.

relationships.title: Dunn and Pesnell v. Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: The complaint challenged Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery’s November 17, 2012 vote adopting its Complaint Commission’s recommendation to institute process and try TE David Swavely. The SJC did not sustain it. Although the record showed possible procedural irregularities—including unauthorized circulation of an earlier complaint—the SJC found no reversible error: presbyteries receive deference on factual records and broad latitude to judge the sufficiency of investigations. The recommendation to proceed to trial stands, subject to later parliamentary action. The SJC did not decide Swavely’s guilt.

The SJC sustained the appeal, reversed the judgment in whole, and dismissed the charges. Once Presbytery denied the member’s complaint, that matter should have ended; moreover, Presbytery did not follow BCO 40-4’s required first step before invoking BCO 40-5 review and control. The delay, prejudice, and missing-witness specifications were moot. The decision did not fault Presbytery’s underlying concern.

The SJC sustained the complaint on procedural grounds: the trial commission relied on his post-indictment exculpatory writings while he declined to testify, depriving the prosecution of cross-examination. The SJC ordered a new trial on the same indictment under specified evidentiary procedures. Because this was a complaint rather than an appeal, it did not reverse the acquittals into findings of guilt or decide the doctrinal merits.

The original complaint had been transmitted to the Faith Church Commission by the Stated Clerk, not committed by Presbytery motion as BCO 15-3 requires, and after the Commission denied it, the Commission did not seek Presbytery approval of its judgment. Because Presbytery had not acted, the SJC complaint was premature; no merits were reached.

relationships.title: Lyons v. Western Carolina Presbytery

topics: BCO 34-2 scandalous charges on slight grounds
metadata.synopsis: Kirk Lyons filed BCO 32-2 charges against TE Craig Bulkeley with Western Carolina Presbytery. WCP dismissed the charges, then ruled Lyons's complaint administratively out of order for lack of standing. The SJC answered that the dismissal was not erroneous—Presbytery had discretion under BCO 31-8, 34-2, and 32-20, and the record showed no clear error—but that WCP erred on standing because Lyons's filing brought him under its jurisdiction. Because that error was not prejudicial, the SJC denied the complaint.

metadata.synopsis: An appellant under suspension from the sacraments challenged the presbytery's judicial commission process and censure. The SJC held the appeal judicially out of order—not decided on the merits—because he had not submitted to a regular trial, as BCO 42-2 requires. Treated as a complaint, it was also out of order: it had not first been presented to the presbytery, and the 30-day period had expired. The SJC further barred complaints about later court actions while he remained under censure, except as to the highest censure. The censure stood.

relationships.title: Ruff v. Nashville Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: Nashville Presbytery's BCO 31-2 investigation of reports against TE George Grant was inadequately documented and internally inconsistent, and the evidence before Presbytery raised a strong presumption of guilt, the SJC held. It sustained the complaint, ruling that pastoral reconciliation does not displace the duty to institute judicial process, and remanded for further proceedings; it did not adjudicate Grant guilty. A concurrence agreed only in remanding to supplement the record under BCO 42-5 & 7.

relationships.title: Sartorious et al. v. Siouxlands Presbytery

topics: fundamentals of the system of doctrine
metadata.synopsis: A complaint challenged Siouxlands Presbytery's investigation of allegations that TE Joshua Moon held heterodox Federal Vision views and its finding of no strong presumption of guilt. The SJC held that Presbytery had investigated diligently under BCO 31-2 and, deferring under BCO 39-3 to its credibility judgment, found no clear error. It declined to decide whether the overture should have been treated as charges because that issue was not raised below, while leaving future charges possible. A concurrence favored charges; the dissent would have found error and remanded.

The SJC vacated the original-jurisdiction mandate because Presbytery had neither found that the Session refused to act nor required the commission to make that finding before proceeding. The authority to receive the reference remained intact; requests from other Sessions alone did not satisfy BCO 33-1.

On remand, Presbytery was to commence process against the elder or rescind that finding and drop the matter. The ruling did not restrict Presbytery’s ability to adopt general position statements outside an investigation.

Steven Wilkins despite his published views on election, the church, perseverance, assurance, and baptism allegedly contradicting the Westminster Standards. The SJC sustained the memorial’s gravity and found Presbytery failed to show due diligence, ordering a recorded examination, formal responses, and report. Presbytery later met the procedural directives, but the SJC relied on Case 2007-8’s substantive finding, cited Presbytery under BCO 40-5, and appointed a prosecutor for Case 2007-14.

metadata.synopsis: Red Mountain Session challenged Presbytery’s ruling that it had inadequately addressed a member’s demand to declare his wife’s divorce unbiblical, and Presbytery’s resulting declaration and Matthew 18 instruction. The SJC sustained all four issues and reversed Presbytery. It held Session’s context-sensitive ruling disclosed no clear error, use of BCO 31-2 was reasonable, Presbytery violated BCO 15-3 by allowing its commission to revise a report after floor discussion, and Presbytery judged the wife without due process. metadata.synopsis: Members challenged Presbytery’s denial of their complaint against a Session instruction not to circulate an open letter repeating allegations against their pastor. The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the instruction in force. It held that liberty of conscience does not eliminate members’ obligation to obey lawful church injunctions. Here the members had sought the Session’s advice, Presbytery had found no strong presumption of chargeable offenses, and renewed circulation would disturb the church’s peace; under those circumstances, the Session acted within its authority.

The SJC sustained both issues: the petition should first have gone to the Session, and Presbytery and its Commission committed additional constitutional errors. Those errors did not excuse his refusal to obey Presbytery, however. Because he had been deposed in Case 2005-8, further action was moot; the SJC granted no remedy, vacatur, or remand.

metadata.synopsis: The St. Paul Session and other Central Florida presbyters complained that Presbytery wrongly sustained a commission report denying the Session complaint and declining to find a strong presumption of guilt against Pastor John Hutchinson. The SJC denied the complaint on both issues. It held CFP permissibly directed a BCO 31-2 investigation and chose its own procedures; procedural irregularities and possible bias did not show BCO 39-3 clear error, though the panel criticized CFP’s handling. A lone dissent would remand, alleging the commission ignored the substance of 41 of 45 specifications.

relationships.title: Fitzsimmons v. Evangel Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: After a church member and deacon was excommunicated by his session, he appealed to Evangel Presbytery. Presbytery found the appeal in order and appointed a commission, but then rescinded that action and never adjudicated the appeal. The SJC held Presbytery erred by failing to notify the appellant of the appeal hearing and by failing to adjudicate an appeal properly before it. It remanded under BCO 42-9 for proper adjudication and made no ruling on the remaining session-related merits issues.

relationships.title: Nickoley v. Rocky Mountain

metadata.synopsis: Rocky Mountain Presbytery cited Pastor Bruce Nickoley for contumacy during his trial, after he allegedly refused to tell his congregation to stop picketing, and immediately deposed him without a hearing. On appeal, the SJC sustained the appeal, holding the Presbytery misapplied BCO provisions on confession, citation, refusal to testify, and deposition; Nickoley neither confessed nor refused to appear. Although presbyteries have general authority to maintain order, serious charges require due process. The SJC remanded, recommending either a new process beginning with BCO §32-3 or revocation of the deposition and reinstatement.

relationships.title: Parks et al. v. Central Carolina Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: Complainants challenged a Session plan under which most elders voluntarily resigned, the Session granted severance and benefits to its former pastor, proposed about a year with an interim pastor before a permanent call, and contemplated revising local bylaws. The SJC denied all four items. It held that the BCO permitted jointly considered voluntary resignations, that severance concerned resignation and the budget rather than a pastoral call, and that the plan and bylaw proposal were not themselves unconstitutional. Any later call still had to follow the BCO without undue delay, and local bylaws had to remain consistent with it.

provisions.title: Section 15-4
provisions.body: The General Assembly shall elect a Standing Judicial Commission to which it shall commit all matters governed by the Rules of Discipline, except for the annual review of Presbytery records, which may come before the Assembly. This commission shall consist of twenty-four (24) members divided into four classes of three teaching elders and three ruling elders in each class. Each class shall serve a four-year term and each subsequent Assembly shall declare the Standing Judicial Commission as a whole to be its commission. Nominations and vacancies shall be filled according to BCO 14-1(11), with nominations allowed from the floor. No person may be elected if there is already a member of the commission from the same Presbytery; but if a person is elected and changes Presbytery, he may continue to serve his full term. No person may serve concurrently on the General Assembly's Standing Judicial Commission and any of the General Assembly's permanent committees.

metadata.synopsis: A ruling elder challenged Session’s elder-term proposal and its creation of Judicial and Governance Commissions. The SJC denied the first two claims: the Constitution does not regulate elder terms, and the Judicial Commission’s assigned business was sufficiently defined. It sustained the Governance Commission claim because sweeping authority and reversed delegation allowed that body to function as Session itself, contrary to BCO 15-1. Session’s third motion was annulled, but Session remained free to adopt a narrower, constitutionally compliant plan.

relationships.title: Speck v. Missouri Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: Speck challenged Missouri Presbytery’s approval of six theological judgments concerning teachings at Revoice 18, its rejection of his procedural point of order, and its refusal to debate gay-couple adoption. The SJC sustained only the first issue, particularly as to Judgments 2, 3, and 5: Presbytery improperly imported BCO 34-5’s ministerial-process standard into court review and then inadequately addressed identified errors affecting church peace and purity. It rejected the procedural and adoption claims and remanded for a focused new hearing under BCO 11-3, 11-4, and 13-9(f).

Steven Wilkins despite his published views on election, the church, perseverance, assurance, and baptism allegedly contradicting the Westminster Standards. metadata.synopsis: In this BCO 40-5 proceeding over Louisiana Presbytery’s investigation of TE Stephen Wilkins, the SJC dismissed Specification 1 because it could not find that the cited procedures were constitutionally required or that guilt was proved. The dismissal did not erase concerns about undocumented doctrinal findings; those failures were covered by Specification 2. On Presbytery’s guilty plea to that specification, the SJC imposed a public admonition for failing to find a strong presumption of doctrinal guilt and pursue trial. Wilkins’s and his church’s withdrawal made practical amends unavailable.

relationships.title: Nickoley and Stephens v. Southwest Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: Complainants challenged Southwest Presbytery's January 1991 actions: withdrawing charges against two ruling elders, dissolving Pastor Pollock's pastoral relationship, and rescinding its suspension of Covenant PC's session. The SJC did not sustain the complaint and affirmed. It held the BCO gives no presbytery authority to suspend a session or act as a Session pro tem without formal congregational consent; BCO 31-1 left the elder charges with the session, so they were never validly before Presbytery; the dissolution challenge was moot after Pollock left the PCA, though Presbytery acted correctly on the congregation's request.

metadata.synopsis: Ruling Elder Chappell complained against Eastern Carolina Presbytery's Commission, which had suspended the session of Fuller Memorial Presbyterian Church and constituted itself as a 'Session Pro Tem' without due process or congregational consent. provisions.title: Section 15-5
provisions.body: a. In the cases committed to it, the Standing Judicial Commission shall have the judicial powers and be governed by the judicial procedures of the General Assembly. The decision of the Standing Judicial Commission shall be the final decision of the General Assembly except as set forth below, to which there may be no complaint or appeal. Members of the Standing Judicial Commission may file concurring or dissenting opinions, or a minority report as set forth in (c) below. The General Assembly may direct the Standing Judicial Commission to retry a case if upon the review of its minutes exceptions are taken with respect to that case. b. In each case the Standing Judicial Commission shall issue a summary of the facts, a statement of the issues, its judgment and its reasoning, together with any concurring or dissenting opinions, all of which shall be entered on the minutes of the General Assembly and shall be reported by the Stated Clerk to the next General Assembly. The judgment shall be effective from the time of its announcement to the parties. c.(1) If, within twenty-four (24) hours of the time of adjournment of a Standing Judicial Commission meeting at which a final decision was rendered in a case, at least one-third (1/3) of the voting members of the Standing Judicial Commission file written notice of their intention to file a minority decision with the Stated Clerk of the General Assembly, and within twenty (20) days from the adjournment do file such a minority decision, such minority decision shall be considered a minority report and shall be referred, with the report of the Standing Judicial Commission, to the General Assembly. In each instance "file" shall be understood as defined by the Operating Manual for Standing Judicial Commission. (2) No such reference* from the Standing Judicial Commission shall be considered by the General Assembly unless the report of the Standing Judicial Commission and the minority report have been mailed to the clerk of Session of each church at least thirty (30) days prior to the meeting of the General Assembly. (3) The Assembly shall act upon such a reference* from the Standing Judicial Commission, in each case without question, discussion, debate, or amendment, as follows: *NOTE: It was the opinion of the 26th General Assembly that "reference" is NOT to be understood as the technical term "reference" in BCO 41-1. (a) The Standing Judicial Commission shall have 30 minutes to present its decision to the Assembly. (b) The minority shall have 30 minutes to present its decision to the Assembly. (c) The Standing Judicial Commission shall have 10 minutes to reply to the minority report. (d) The decision of the minority shall be proposed and the General Assembly shall, without question, discussion, debate, or amendment approve or disapprove of the minority report. (e) If the General Assembly disapproves the minority report, the General Assembly shall take up the decision of the Standing Judicial Commission and without question, discussion, debate, or amendment, approve or disapprove of the decision of the Standing Judicial Commission. (4) If the General Assembly approves of a proposed decision, it shall be the decision of the General Assembly, and printed in its minutes. There may be no complaint or appeal from such a final decision of the General Assembly. If the General Assembly finally disapproves of both proposed decisions, it must set the case for hearing before the General Assembly or a special commission appointed by it, and in either instance the case shall be tried on the record as delivered to the Stated Clerk. Any such special commission shall then proceed to consider the case and shall report its decision, in like manner, to the General Assembly for its approval or disapproval. In any event, the full record of the case, including written testimony of witnesses, all documents, exhibits and papers shall be delivered to the Stated Clerk for permanent preservation.

relationships.title: Bulkeley & Gillikin v. Highlands Presbytery

occurrences.excerpt: BCO 15-5.a establishes that “the Standing Judicial Commission shall have the judicial powers and be governed by the judicial procedures of the General Assembly."

metadata.synopsis: TEs Bulkeley and Gillikin complained that Highlands Presbytery refused to record their dissent against Presbytery's act of recording a letter from the Arden Presbyterian Session affirming the Martins' Christian character. The SJC denied the complaint but went further, annulling Presbytery's recording of the Session letter as contrary to BCO 14-7 and the finality of the prior Sheppard decision (Case 2022-04), generating multiple concurring and dissenting opinions about the SJC's authority to reach issues not raised by the parties.

relationships.title: DeJong v. Session of Village Seven Presbyterian Church

metadata.synopsis: A ruling elder challenged Session’s elder-term proposal and its creation of Judicial and Governance Commissions. The SJC denied the first two claims: the Constitution does not regulate elder terms, and the Judicial Commission’s assigned business was sufficiently defined. It sustained the Governance Commission claim because sweeping authority and reversed delegation allowed that body to function as Session itself, contrary to BCO 15-1. Session’s third motion was annulled, but Session remained free to adopt a narrower, constitutionally compliant plan.

relationships.title: Speck v. Missouri Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: Speck challenged Missouri Presbytery’s approval of six theological judgments concerning teachings at Revoice 18, its rejection of his procedural point of order, and its refusal to debate gay-couple adoption. The SJC sustained only the first issue, particularly as to Judgments 2, 3, and 5: Presbytery improperly imported BCO 34-5’s ministerial-process standard into court review and then inadequately addressed identified errors affecting church peace and purity. It rejected the procedural and adoption claims and remanded for a focused new hearing under BCO 11-3, 11-4, and 13-9(f).

metadata.synopsis: After her session erased her from the roll, Anna Lewis filed a BCO 40-5 report directly with the SJC, alleging the Presbytery of the Mississippi Valley failed to redress the session's alleged failure to give BCO 38-4 notice. The SJC held the filing out of order: under RAO 16-10.c and OMSJC Chapter 15, BCO Chapter 40 matters come to it only by General Assembly referral. It did not decide the merits, but noted that without proper notice Lewis remains a member unless she joined another church. Dissents disputed that limitation and cited past direct reviews.

metadata.synopsis: TE James Bachmann appealed Nashville Presbytery's decision to replace his judicial commission's recommended admonition with indefinite suspension. The SJC sustained the appeal: Presbytery violated BCO 15-3 by dividing the verdict and amending the censure, which it had to approve or disapprove as a whole without debate. Bachmann's earlier procedural challenges were not sustained; his unconditional post-trial confession waived them. The SJC rendered the commission's judgment and admonition as its own decision, remanded to Presbytery, and restored Bachmann to good standing, subject to possible pastoral oversight items 2–4.

metadata.synopsis: The SJC denied a complaint challenging Nashville Presbytery's decision not to indict a teaching elder for allegedly sinful teaching on homosexuality and same-sex attraction. The adopted judgment held that the 147-page record showed Presbytery fulfilled its BCO 31-2 investigatory duty and did not show it erred in judgment when it declined process; the complaint was denied 20-0-1. Concurring opinions raised concerns about committee recusal, record clarity, and exegetical uses of Scripture, but they were separate and did not alter the denial.

metadata.synopsis: Did a presbytery violate the BCO or clearly err by dissolving a congregation without its consent? The SJC said no and denied the complaint. On the constitutional issue, it held that BCO 13-9.f grants dissolution power and BCO 40-6 does not impose formal process for it. On the discretionary issue, it found no clear error in the record. The denial left dissolution in place and warned that such action still requires sufficient justification and prudent, reviewable procedure.

No merits review appears; the adopted vote was 18 concurring, 2 not qualified, and 4 absent.

metadata.synopsis: An individual appealed directly to the SJC, alleging her church effectively excommunicated her without process, failed the Matthew 18 process, and spiritually abused her by social isolation. The SJC dismissed as premature, without reaching the merits, because there was no record of a judicial decision by the church or of an appeal to Evangel Presbytery, the next higher court; it stated she could proceed only by providing such evidence. The severity of excommunication did not excuse that prerequisite. The SJC asked Presbytery to obtain the session's written response to her letter.

relationships.title: Snapp v. James River Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: The complaint challenged James River Presbytery's approval of an ordination examination in which the candidate called the Genesis creation days God's anthropomorphic work days, not necessarily twenty-four-hour days. The complainant argued that view conflicted with WCF I.9. The SJC denied the complaint and answered 'No' to whether the Presbytery erred; the examination stood. It held the Presbytery had authority and discretion, no General Assembly had declared anthropomorphic days contrary to the Standards, and an advisory-committee study left the SJC unwilling to decide creation-day length. A six-member dissent sought an exception and study-committee referral.

metadata.synopsis: Mt. Carmel Session challenged New Jersey Presbytery's creation-days resolution, arguing that the Westminster Standards require six consecutive twenty-four-hour days. The SJC majority concluded that Presbytery could resolve the doctrinal question under BCO 11-4 and that prior Assembly actions permitted latitude on the length of the creation days. The General Assembly rejected the minority report, adopted the majority report, and denied the complaint.

relationships.title: Session of Harvestwood PCA v. New River Presbytery (Complaint)

metadata.synopsis: New River Presbytery treated Grace Covenant PCA's BCO 41 inquiry about a Sunday school teacher's acceptability as a request for advice, but then ruled he was eligible to teach. On Harvestwood's complaint, the SJC held that Presbytery lacked original jurisdiction to make that final disposition and that the record was unclear about the teacher's views. The SJC sustained the complaint and recommended that Presbytery rescind its March 15, 1997 action and clarify his views through proper BCO procedures; it declined to reach the creation and theistic-evolution merits.

The SJC agreed that Presbytery should have acknowledged and noted the exceptions, but upheld the examination. It found no proof that Blaha’s denial that the gifts conveyed revelation crossed prior Assembly limits and deferred to Presbytery on an unsettled issue. It expressly declined reexamination or remand; a substantial partial dissent would have set the examination aside.

The SJC denied the first item because BCO 31-2 permits declining process when investigation raises no strong presumption of guilt. It sustained the second: jurisdiction properly invoked while a communicant member is not lost through a later status change. No remand was expressly ordered.

metadata.synopsis: A congregation member complained that New River Presbytery erred in November 1991 by declining to accept TE Don Post Jr.'s resignation and dissolve his pastoral relation, instead appointing a commission. The SJC sustained the complaint. Under BCO 23-1, once the congregation concurred and no sufficient reasons to retain the pastor appeared, the resignation 'shall be accepted' and the relation dissolved; the Presbytery's general BCO 13-9 power did not override that specific provision. The Presbytery had already dissolved the relation on December 7, 1991; the adopted judgment ordered no remand. Three commissioners dissented.

metadata.synopsis: Smith challenged Northeast Presbytery’s ruling that his complaint was untimely and unconstitutional after it dissolved Grace Church and indefinitely postponed a proposed Braintree mission. The SJC sustained the complaint and remanded it for Presbytery adjudication. The May action first revealed Presbytery’s view that former members were outside the PCA, so the June complaint was timely. BCO 11-4 neither barred nor itself required care; responsibility arose here from the April referral to Presbytery’s missions committee. Care need not take the form of a mission, and mere dissolution alone would not create that responsibility.

metadata.synopsis: Two ruling-elder nominees challenged the Session’s refusal to approve them based on their theonomic views and perceived divisiveness. The full SJC denied the complaint, holding that the court of original jurisdiction may assess an unsettled theological position and whether it threatens the church’s peace, purity, or progress; divisiveness was therefore properly considered. The ruling did not decide the merits of theonomy itself, and it left undisturbed Presbytery’s annulment of the Session’s categorical statement that theonomy violated WCF 19.4.

provisions.title: Chapter 16 · Church Orders – The Doctrine of Vocation
provisions.body:
BCO 16-1

Ordinary vocation to office in the Church is the calling of God by the Spirit, through the inward testimony of a good conscience, the manifest approbation of God's people, and the concurring judgment of a lawful court of the Church.

BCO 16-2

The government of the Church is by officers gifted to represent Christ, and the right of God's people to recognize by election to office those so gifted is inalienable. Therefore no man can be placed over a church in any office without the election, or at least the consent of that church.

BCO 16-3

Upon those whom God calls to bear office in His Church He bestows suitable gifts for the discharge of their various duties. And it is indispensable that, besides possessing the necessary gifts and abilities, natural and acquired, every one admitted to an office should be sound in the faith, and his life be according to godliness. Wherefore every candidate for office is to be approved by the court by which he is to be ordained.

BCO 16-4

Officers in the Presbyterian Church in America must be above reproach in their walk and Christlike in their character. While office bearers will see spiritual perfection only in glory, they will continue in this life to confess and to mortify remaining sins in light of God's work of progressive sanctification. Therefore, to be qualified for office, they must affirm the sinfulness of fallen desires, the reality and hope of progressive sanctification, and be committed to the pursuit of Spirit-empowered victory over their sinful temptations, inclinations, and actions.

metadata.synopsis: Grace PCA’s Session challenged Ohio Presbytery’s reversal of excommunication for two members convicted of heresy. The SJC partially sustained the complaint: prior indefinite suspension was not constitutionally required, but Presbytery properly found excommunication too severe because the trial record contained no evidence of contumacy. Presbytery nevertheless had to impose an appropriate lesser censure or remand for one, and lacked authority to mandate transfer to another church. The unappealed heresy convictions remained, but because the members had joined another church, further proceedings were moot.

metadata.synopsis: The SJC addressed whether a presbytery and its administrative/judicial commission could suspend a local session and assume original jurisdiction over charges against a ruling elder. It answered no: original jurisdiction belonged to the session, and a presbytery cannot "act for" a lower court by replacing congregationally elected elders. Preliminary Principle Six, BCO 16-2, and BCO 31-1/33-1 controlled; the commission's interpretation of BCO 13-9 conflicted with those principles. The Presbytery's and Commission's actions, including the censure approved by Presbytery, were reversed.

provisions.body: Upon those whom God calls to bear office in His Church He bestows suitable gifts for the discharge of their various duties. And it is indispensable that, besides possessing the necessary gifts and abilities, natural and acquired, every one admitted to an office should be sound in the faith, and his life be according to godliness. Wherefore every candidate for office is to be approved by the court by which he is to be ordained.

relationships.title: Jones v. Louisiana

metadata.synopsis: Louisiana Presbytery’s refusal to institute process after examining Steve Wilkins’s Federal Vision teachings was challenged for applying the wrong constitutional standard and overlooking a strong presumption that some views were out of conformity with the Westminster Standards. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled Presbytery’s denial. A “difference” need not expressly contradict the Standards; Presbytery must independently investigate and classify it rather than accept the member’s assurance or shift the burden to objectors. The ruling did not adjudicate Wilkins’s guilt; the Central Carolina memorial remained before the SJC.

provisions.title: Section 16-4
provisions.body: Officers in the Presbyterian Church in America must be above reproach in their walk and Christlike in their character. While office bearers will see spiritual perfection only in glory, they will continue in this life to confess and to mortify remaining sins in light of God's work of progressive sanctification. Therefore, to be qualified for office, they must affirm the sinfulness of fallen desires, the reality and hope of progressive sanctification, and be committed to the pursuit of Spirit-empowered victory over their sinful temptations, inclinations, and actions.

metadata.synopsis: Brown challenged Presbytery’s abstract approval of six views concerning diaconal practice. The SJC sustained the consolidated complaints and annulled Presbytery’s action because a church court cannot issue a binding decree apart from properly exercising jurisdiction over specific persons. Constitutional conformity must instead be determined through authorized examination or judicial processes. The judgment deliberately left unresolved whether any of the six views themselves were faithful to the Constitution; the detailed view-by-view analysis appeared only in a concurring opinion.

metadata.synopsis: Two consolidated complaints challenged Philadelphia Presbytery’s licensing and ordination of a candidate who believed Scripture could permit women to hold the deacon’s office but promised to follow the BCO and not ordain women. The SJC denied both complaints and affirmed Presbytery. It distinguished subscription to doctrinal standards from approval of BCO practices, applied a three-part inquiry, and deferred to Presbytery on the candidate’s credible vow. Because complainants identified no violated doctrinal standard, no error was shown. The ruling reaffirmed that the BCO bars ordaining women as deacons.
